# **Technical Architecture and Design Specification of the LAX Autopilot Liquidation Engine**

## **System Topology and Integration Framework**

The LAX Autopilot Liquidation Engine is an autonomous, terminal-driven monitoring and execution system optimized for local simulation using an Anvil fork of Base mainnet1. The topology bridges an interactive command-line interface to the execution layer of the KeeperHub Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, translating real-time agentic decisions into guaranteed on-chain transactions1. In high-frequency, competitive liquidation environments, transaction latency, inclusion guarantees, and structural gas optimization represent the primary vectors of competitive advantage. The LAX architecture resolves these challenges by establishing a stateful middleware layer that integrates Turnkey-backed secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) wallets, dual-routing micro-payment mechanisms (x402 and Multi-Party Payments), and intelligent transaction orchestration pipelines directly with liquidity protocol deployments on Base1.  
To facilitate high-fidelity testing and ensure robust handling of edge cases under simulated market anomalies, the LAX Autopilot operates against a local Anvil node mirroring Base mainnet state. This local execution environment communicates directly with Aave V3 deployments on Base. Telemetry and state updates are ingested via the Aave Protocol Data Provider contract located at 0x9390B1735def18560c509E2d0bc090E9d6BA257a, while pool configurations and proxy references are retrieved dynamically from the PoolAddressesProvider registry at 0xa234E48961C34e6fC2D96d2b3bc3E8792D6Ac457563. The CLI intercepts system operator inputs, synthesizes transaction requirements, and outputs structured JSON payloads compatible with the KeeperHub MCP standard4. The KeeperHub REST API and MCP server then orchestrate the on-chain execution, bypassing manual wallet management and raw private key exposure while maintaining an append-only audit trail1.  
The economic settlement of transactions within this framework utilizes a dual-protocol billing engine. The system supports micro-payments settled on-chain via the x402 standard using Base USDC, or via Tempo Multi-Party Payments (MPP) utilizing USDC.e, routing through turn-key backed custody accounts equipped with automatic safety hooks1. This multi-tiered structural design ensures that the autonomous autopilot agent can self-fund its operations, cover local gas costs, pay for execution fees, and process liquidations with deterministic inclusion guarantees1.

The structural foundation of KeeperHub is rooted in enterprise-grade DeFi DevOps patterns, designed specifically to replace fragile local scripts and exposed plaintext private keys with managed workflow automation infrastructure11. Operating as a unified execution system, KeeperHub orchestrates transactions across multiple target protocols using visual builders, scheduled cron-based triggers, webhook event hooks, and direct smart contract listeners5. Developers can transition from visual prototyping to programmatic execution by exporting workflows directly into type-safe TypeScript code blocks via the "use workflow" framework directive5. This hybrid workflow architecture is implemented via a modern Web3 technology stack utilizing Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript 5, and PostgreSQL with a Drizzle ORM layer, supported by a specialized Workflow DevKit execution engine5.  
For autonomous entities, integration is supported across major agent frameworks, including ElizaOS, OpenClaw, LangChain, and CrewAI, utilizing unified SDK wrappers that expose Web3 transaction interfaces to plain-English prompts1. When an AI agent decides to execute an action, the underlying SDK translates the natural language instruction into structured calls to the KeeperHub MCP server, which manages state transitions, simulates outcomes, enforces spending limits, and optimizes transaction fee parameters1.

## **Advanced Engineering Foundations**

### **Maximal Extractable Value Protection and Private Routing**

Liquidations are competitive, zero-sum processes where public mempool submission exposes transactions to frontrunning, backrunning, and sandwich attacks. The LAX Autopilot mitigates this vulnerability by integrating directly with KeeperHub’s private routing interface1. When a liquidation command is dispatched, the raw transaction payload is bypassed from the public Base mempool and routed directly to private block-builder endpoints using Flashbots-style RPC tunnels1. This ensures that competitive liquidation transactions remain invisible to public MEV searchers until they are durably included in a block.  
The platform combines this private pathing with intelligent gas fee estimation featuring exponential backoff, which adjusts to sudden network congestion events1. The system programmatically polls the Base L2 gas price oracle to compute baseline fees, applying an escalating multiplier during high-competition blocks1. The mathematical formulation for the transaction-inclusion gas price (![][image1]) under escalating network congestion is expressed as:  
![][image2]  
where ![][image3] represents the base fee of the network, ![][image4] is the tip fee paid to the validator to incentivize rapid block inclusion, ![][image5] is the dynamic congestion fee calculated from the L2 oracle, ![][image6] is the escalation margin percentage, and ![][image7] is the consecutive transaction retry count. This gas escalation logic ensures that the autopilot outpaces competitive keepers while avoiding overpaying during momentary gas spikes1.

### **Stateful Health Recovery and Position Self-Healing**

The stateful health recovery mechanism prevents the liquidation of the operator’s own collateralized debt positions by monitoring health indicators on-chain9. By polling the Protocol Data Provider contract, the engine calculates the real-time Health Factor (![][image8]) of registered accounts13. The formal definition of the Aave V3 Health Factor is calculated as follows:  
![][image9]  
where ![][image10] is the value of collateral asset ![][image11] in base reference currency, ![][image12] is the liquidation threshold of asset ![][image11], and ![][image13] is the value of debt asset ![][image14] in the reference currency13. If the calculated ![][image8] drops below a user-configured critical threshold (e.g., ![][image15]), the autopilot triggers an automated self-healing protocol.  
This sequence is executed via KeeperHub workflows that utilize the Aave V3 Position Manager or Credit Delegation features9. Under the Aave V3.4 specification, the position manager interface allows users to approve a specific management contract (using approvePositionManager) to execute risk-mitigating actions like setUserUseReserveAsCollateralOnBehalfOf and setUserEModeOnBehalfOf14. To minimize gas during volatile liquidations, the V3.4 upgrade optimizes these paths by converting storage-heavy configurations into immutables—such as RESERVE\_INTEREST\_RATE\_STRATEGY on the core Pool contract, REWARDS\_CONTROLLER on the base token contract, and the static pool reference on the Protocol Data Provider14.  
To further secure these calculations against arbitrage and precision-loss attacks, the Aave V3.5 upgrade introduces strict rounding logic16. When the self-healing system or an external competitor burns variable debt tokens during a liquidation, the protocol applies explicit rounding directions to prevent fractional asset leakage16. This is mathematically represented by the ceil-division of the protocol's liquidation fee over the pool's liquidity index16:  
![][image16]  
This ensures that the protocol does not burn more debt than the underlying collateral can back, preserving systemic solvency16.

### **Automated Portfolio Rebalancing**

Yield and risk exposure are optimized through the automated rebalancing engine17. The system integrates with an external smart contract architecture, allowing the CLI to adjust portfolio allocation basis points (BPS) dynamically based on live APY metrics and risk assessments17. The target allocation vector for each asset ![][image11] is calculated such that:  
![][image17]  
When live performance metrics deviate from the fitness parameters, the autopilot updates the BPS values and triggers a KeeperHub automated workflow17. This initiates the withdrawal of capital from lower-performing or higher-risk reserves and reallocates the freed liquidity into optimal target pools, maximizing capital efficiency while maintaining protective supply and borrow caps18.

## **Flow Mechanics and Execution Mappings**

The transaction lifecycle of a CLI command begins at the interactive terminal and is processed through several system modules before execution on-chain1. Below is the systematic transaction path from command parsing to execution within the local Anvil fork:

\[Interactive CLI\]  
       │  
       ▼ (Parses command & payload, e.g., "lax exec liquidate")  
\[KeeperHub MCP Client Wrapper\]  
       │  
       ▼ (Translates CLI parameters to KeeperHub tool format over Stdio/HTTP)  
\[KeeperHub MCP Server\]  
       │  
       ▼ (Performs signature check, simulation, and gas optimization)  
\[Turnkey-backed MPC Platform\]  
       │  
       ▼ (Generates & signs transaction payload via Para MPC wallet)  
\[Private MEV Route Relay\]  
       │  
       ▼ (Bypasses public mempool to avoid searcher frontrunning)  
\[Anvil Fork (Base Mainnet State)\]  
       │  
       ▼ (Executes transaction against Aave V3 Core contracts)  
\[Execution Log Sink\]  
       │  
       ▼ (Returns transaction receipt & appends to KeeperHub Audit Trail)  
\[CLI UI / Output Stream\]

When an operator issues a liquidation command, the CLI formats the inputs into a structured JSON payload for the MCP client4. The client routes this to the local MCP server, which interfaces with KeeperHub's cloud infrastructure4. The system simulates the transaction on the target network state to verify viability and prevent reverts1. If the simulation succeeds, the transaction is signed using a Para MPC wallet, which maintains key security by using distributed MPC shares with no single point of private key exposure5. The signed transaction payload is then routed through private RPC endpoints to the Anvil node1. Once executed on the fork, the block state updates, and a transaction hash is returned1. The execution logs are appended to the audit trail, and the CLI terminal updates with execution status, block number, gas used, and liquidation profit margins1.

## **Three-Minute Automated Demonstration Script**

This demonstration script models an automated liquidation event on an Anvil fork of Base mainnet. The scenario simulates a sudden market shock where a target user's collateral value falls, dropping their health factor below 1.0 and triggering the liquidation autopilot13.

### **Terminal Initialization and State Simulation**

The operator boots the local Anvil fork of Base mainnet and configures the tracking targets.

Bash  
\# Terminal Time: 0:00 \- 0:45  
\# Step 1: Initialize Anvil Fork of Base mainnet at block 15,998,883  
$ lax config anvil-fork \--rpc-url https://mainnet.base.org \--block-number 15998883  
\[SUCCESS\] Anvil fork initialized successfully. Local RPC: http://127.0.0.1:8545. Forking chain ID 8453\.

\# Step 2: Establish connection to KeeperHub MCP Server  
$ export KEEPERHUB\_API\_KEY=kh\_sec\_9281a0ff8e7b1a  
$ docker run \-i \--rm \-e KEEPERHUB\_API\_KEY keeperhub-mcp  
\[SUCCESS\] Connected to KeeperHub MCP Server. Organization: Delta-Alpha-Ops. Agentic Wallets: Active.

\# Step 3: Monitor target account health telemetry  
$ lax check user-config \--user 0x7aE2930B50CFEbc99FE6DB16CE5B9C7D8d09332C  
\[TELEMETRY\] Querying Aave V3 Protocol Data Provider on Base...  
Account: 0x7aE2930B50CFEbc99FE6DB16CE5B9C7D8d09332C

Total Debt (Base):        9,800.00 USD  
Current LTV:              80.00%  
Liquidation Threshold:    85.00%  
Health Factor (HF):       1.084  
Status: HEALTHY

### **Simulating a Market Shock and Dry-Run Verification**

The operator simulates a market drop in WETH to push the target account into insolvency.

Bash  
\# Terminal Time: 0:45 \- 1:30  
\# Step 4: Inject market price shock to trigger insolvency (force drop WETH price by 15%)  
$ lax config cheat-price \--asset 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000006 \--price 2890.50  
\[CHEATCODE\] Overriding Chainlink Price Oracle feed for asset WETH9 on Anvil local node.  
Previous Price: 3400.00 USD \-\> New Price: 2890.50 USD. Block time warped \+12s.

\# Step 5: Check health factor post-shock to verify target is liquidatable  
$ lax check health \--user 0x7aE2930B50CFEbc99FE6DB16CE5B9C7D8d09332C  
\[ALERT\] Account Health Factor has breached the liquidation threshold\!  
Current Health Factor: 0.921  
Liquidatable Debt Volume: 4,900.00 USD (equivalent to 50.00% close factor)

\# Step 6: Simulate the liquidation locally to verify execution viability  
$ lax simulate liquidate \--user 0x7aE2930B50CFEbc99FE6DB16CE5B9C7D8d09332C \\  
                         \--collateral 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000006 \\  
                         \--debt 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bda02913 \\  
                         \--debt-to-cover 4900000000  
\[SIMULATION\] Dry-run execution success on Anvil block 15,998,884.  
Estimated Gas: 145,210 Gwei  
Execution Status: SUCCESS  
Seized Collateral: 1.84 WETH  
Liquidation Penalty: 5.00% (Profit: \~245.00 USD)

### **Launching Automated Liquidation and Confirming Audit Trail**

The autopilot triggers the transaction through KeeperHub's execution layer with MEV protection1.

Bash  
\# Terminal Time: 1:30 \- 3:00  
\# Step 7: Disarm competitor bots by routing transaction via private MEV pathways  
$ lax set mev-routing \--enable true \--provider flashbots  
\[CONFIG\] Private MEV Routing enabled. Transactions bypassed from public mempools.

\# Step 8: Execute the on-chain liquidation with priority gas pricing

                     \--collateral 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000006 \\

                     \--debt-to-cover 4900000000 \\

## **Technical Criteria Mapping**

The architecture of the LAX Autopilot Liquidation Engine is structured to meet and exceed the strict evaluation guidelines of high-performance Web3 agent environments1. The table below maps these specific technical requirements to the system's operational features.

| Hackathon Criterion | System Capability | Implementation & Architecture Specifics |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Execution Completeness** | Live On-Chain Transactions | Real transactions are executed on an Anvil fork of Base mainnet, which replicates exact state1. Transactions avoid mock data and process directly via the Aave V3 Core contracts3. |
| **KeeperHub Integration Depth** | Multi-Surface Stack Usage | Utilizes the KeeperHub MCP server, CLI wrapper, @keeperhub/sdk, and x402/MPP micro-payments inside the agentic wallet infrastructure1. |
| **Reliability & Observability** | Stuck Transaction Prevention & Logs | Implements dynamic gas tracking via the Base Gas Price Oracle, paired with exponential backoff and retries to handle network congestion1. The system also maintains an audit trail with execution logs1. |
| **DeFi Engineering Rigor** | Advanced Risk Management | Features Flashbots-style private RPC routing for MEV protection, automated self-healing for health factor drops, and live BPS adjustments for rebalancing1. |

## **Strategic Technical Conclusions**

Integrating an interactive CLI with the KeeperHub workflow automation stack provides a robust infrastructure for autonomous DeFi agents1. By wrapping complex contract interactions into structured, low-level tooling commands, developers can build agents that operate safely and predictably on-chain5. The system design addresses the primary failure modes of DeFi automation—including frontrunning risks, transaction inclusion delays, and key exposure—by utilizing private routing, intelligent gas pricing, and Para MPC key management1. Operating these tools within a local Anvil environment that mirrors Base mainnet state allows developers to thoroughly test agent strategies and liquidation routines under simulated market shocks1. This architecture provides a production-grade template for building reliable, autonomous liquidation engines on Base.
